headline: A new study co-written by MIT economist David Autor found that AI raised the quality of patent lawyers' drafts but improved their skill without AI only among experienced lawyers.
score_reason: Pool 5 kept: carefully caveated findings, but unreviewed, Google-run and limited to one profession.
importance_line: Early-career professionals, and employers tempted to hire fewer juniors because AI lifts output, are most affected, since the result suggests juniors who lean on AI may not build the skills; it is a small, short, Google-run study of one profession that has not been peer-reviewed, it did not study Gen Z as a group, and it does not show that AI stops juniors becoming experts over a career.
summary: Fortune reports on a National Bureau of Economic Research working paper, not yet peer-reviewed, co-written by MIT economist David Autor with six Google employees and paid for by Google, in which 133 patent lawyers at 11 firms were randomly given an AI drafting assistant: after 90 days AI users' drafts scored higher, but in a test without AI only senior lawyers beat their unassisted peers, while junior lawyers showed no average gain. Autor told Fortune that AI is a 'performance equalizer' but a 'skill-disequalizer' and warned young professionals of an 'illusion of competence'; the paper's own limits include a small sample, only 91 of the 133 finishing the unaided test, no skills test at the start and just three months of use.
notes: Whole Fortune article read. The paper's own date is not given in Fortune's text.
